concepts.name: Definition of a Database
concepts.summary: A database is a logically coherent, purposefully designed collection of related data that represents some aspect of a real-world 'miniworld,' not just any random data.

misconceptions.name: Any Collection of Data is a Database
misconceptions.description: Students think any random assortment of stored data qualifies as a database, ignoring the requirement of logical coherence and inherent meaning.
misconceptions.wrong_model: If I just dump a bunch of unrelated numbers and words into a file, that file counts as a database because it's data.
misconceptions.correct_model: A database must be a logically coherent collection of data with inherent meaning, representing some aspect of the real world for a specific purpose.

misconceptions.name: Database Confused with DBMS
misconceptions.description: Students conflate the database (the stored data itself) with the DBMS (the software that manages it), treating them as the same thing.
misconceptions.wrong_model: The database and the DBMS are basically the same thing—when I say 'database' I mean the software like MySQL.
misconceptions.correct_model: The database is the actual stored data; the DBMS is the software that creates, manages, and provides access to that data. Together they form a database system.

misconceptions.name: Database as a Static, One-Time Record
misconceptions.description: Students believe a database is a fixed snapshot of information rather than something that must be continuously updated to reflect real-world changes.
misconceptions.wrong_model: Once we build the database and load the data in, it stays accurate forever unless someone manually decides to redo it.
misconceptions.correct_model: A database must be updated as soon as possible whenever real-world events or transactions occur so it remains an accurate reflection of the miniworld.

concepts.name: DBMS (Database Management System)
concepts.summary: A DBMS is general-purpose software that enables defining, constructing, manipulating, sharing, and protecting a database, distinct from the data or from application-specific programs.

misconceptions.name: DBMS Just Stores Data
misconceptions.description: Students think the DBMS's only job is physically storing data on disk, missing its roles in defining structure, manipulation, sharing, and protection.
misconceptions.wrong_model: A DBMS is just a program that saves my data to the hard drive, nothing more.
misconceptions.correct_model: A DBMS defines data structures/constraints, constructs storage, manipulates data via queries and updates, shares data among users, and protects/maintains it long-term.

misconceptions.name: A Database Must Use a General-Purpose DBMS
misconceptions.description: Students believe that without commercial DBMS software (like Oracle or MySQL), you cannot have a database at all.
misconceptions.wrong_model: You can't have a real database unless you're using an official DBMS product—writing your own programs to manage data doesn't count.
misconceptions.correct_model: A computerized database can be managed either by a general-purpose DBMS or by custom-written application programs acting as a special-purpose DBMS.

misconceptions.name: Queries and Transactions Are the Same Thing
misconceptions.description: Students use 'query' and 'transaction' interchangeably, not recognizing that queries retrieve data while transactions may involve both reading and writing data.
misconceptions.wrong_model: A query and a transaction are the same thing—both just mean 'asking the database something.'
misconceptions.correct_model: A query typically retrieves data, while a transaction may involve both reading data and writing/modifying data in the database.

concepts.name: Meta-data and the Database Catalog
concepts.summary: Meta-data is the self-describing information (structure, types, constraints) about the database, stored in a catalog by the DBMS, separate from the actual data records.

misconceptions.name: Meta-data Confused with Regular Data
misconceptions.description: Students think meta-data refers to the actual records (like student names and grades) rather than the descriptive information about the database's structure.
misconceptions.wrong_model: Meta-data just means all the data stored in the database, like the student names and grades.
misconceptions.correct_model: Meta-data is descriptive information about the database's structure—data types, formats, and constraints—stored separately in the catalog, not the actual records themselves.

misconceptions.name: Catalog Is an Optional Add-on
misconceptions.description: Students believe the database catalog/dictionary is an extra convenience feature rather than a fundamental, defining characteristic of the database approach.
misconceptions.wrong_model: The catalog with all the structure info is just a nice-to-have feature some DBMSs include, not something essential.
misconceptions.correct_model: The self-describing nature via the catalog is a fundamental characteristic of the database approach, distinguishing it from traditional file processing.

misconceptions.name: Applications Define Meta-data Independently
misconceptions.description: Students think each application program can define its own version of the data structure/types, similar to how file-processing systems let each program name data independently.
misconceptions.wrong_model: Each application that uses the database can set up its own definitions for the data fields, like in old file systems.
misconceptions.correct_model: In the database approach, data names and structures are defined once in the catalog and used consistently by all queries, transactions, and applications.

concepts.name: Database Approach vs. Traditional File Processing
concepts.summary: The database approach centralizes data in a single repository accessed by multiple applications, eliminating the redundancy and separate file maintenance typical of traditional file-processing systems.

misconceptions.name: File Processing Is Just as Good as Databases
misconceptions.description: Students think there's no real downside to each application maintaining its own separate files, missing the redundancy and maintenance problems this causes.
misconceptions.wrong_model: It doesn't matter if the grade office and the accounting office each keep their own separate student files—that's basically the same as using a shared database.
misconceptions.correct_model: Traditional file processing causes redundant data storage and duplicated maintenance effort, which the database approach avoids through a single shared repository.

misconceptions.name: Databases Are for Single-User Access Only
misconceptions.description: Students fail to recognize that a defining feature of the database approach is supporting simultaneous multiuser access and multiple views of data.
misconceptions.wrong_model: A database is basically just one big file that one program at a time reads from, similar to a regular file.
misconceptions.correct_model: The database approach supports sharing of data among multiple users and programs simultaneously, along with multiple views of the same underlying data.

misconceptions.name: Data Redundancy Across Files Is Unavoidable/Necessary
misconceptions.description: Students think that because different departments need different data about the same entity (e.g., students), it's necessary and normal for each to keep fully separate, duplicated files.
misconceptions.wrong_model: Since the grade office and accounting office need different information about students, they just have to keep completely separate files with overlapping data—there's no other way.
misconceptions.correct_model: The database approach lets a single repository store data once, defined centrally, while still letting different users/applications access the relevant parts they need, avoiding redundant storage.

concepts.name: Structure and Relationships in a Database (e.g., UNIVERSITY example)
concepts.summary: A database organizes data into multiple related files/tables (like STUDENT, COURSE, SECTION, GRADE_REPORT, PREREQUISITE), where records in different files are connected through shared fields.

misconceptions.name: Files in a Database Are Independent of Each Other
misconceptions.description: Students think each file (STUDENT, COURSE, etc.) stands alone with no meaningful connection to other files, missing the relational linking via keys like Student_number or Course_number.
misconceptions.wrong_model: The STUDENT file and the GRADE_REPORT file are separate things with no real connection—they just happen to be in the same database.
misconceptions.correct_model: Records across files are related through shared identifiers (e.g., Student_number links STUDENT to GRADE_REPORT), and most real databases have many such relationships among records.

misconceptions.name: Record Structure Doesn't Need Formal Definition
misconceptions.description: Students believe you can just start entering data without first specifying the data types and structure of each field.
misconceptions.wrong_model: You can just start typing student names and numbers into the database; you don't need to define ahead of time what type each field is.
misconceptions.correct_model: Before constructing the database, you must define the structure of each record by specifying the data elements and their data types (e.g., Name as a string, Student_number as an integer).

misconceptions.name: Coded Values Are Arbitrary and Don't Need Consistent Meaning
misconceptions.description: Students think coded values like Class=1,2,3 are just arbitrary labels that can mean different things in different contexts, rather than a consistently defined coding scheme.
misconceptions.wrong_model: The number 1 for Class could mean freshman in one record and something else in another—it's just a random label.
misconceptions.correct_model: A coding scheme (e.g., 1=freshman, 2=sophomore) is defined consistently as part of the database structure so that coded values have the same meaning throughout.
